hook_text: In 1860 a country with two people in every hundred on Earth made half the world's iron and coal. How?
clip_script: London, 1851. A palace of glass, three hundred thousand panes, full of steam engines and locomotives. Britain is showing off, and it has reason to. Coal and iron sit side by side underground. Inventors build machines that do the work of dozens. Banks lend, railways race, steamships cross oceans. The Royal Navy, bigger than the next two or three navies combined, guards the sea lanes, including the Cape on the road to India. But follow the cotton thread back. It was picked by enslaved people in America. Indian weavers lost their trade. And soon Belgium, France and Germany caught up, and the rival powers turned their steamships and machine guns on Africa. Industrial wealth and empire were two sides of the same coin.
visual_style: A whiteboard glass palace sketched with a single line, a factory chimney, a ship circling a globe, then a cotton thread running back to a field and forward to a map of Africa being cut into pieces.
pacing: Fast and bright through the exhibition and the machines, slowing sharply at the cotton thread.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and see who paid for the workshop of the world.
